faq.a: Parasympathetic fibers lie peripherally and are compressed first; ischemic infarcts affect the central motor core, sparing the pupil.
faq.q: Why is the pupil often dilated in compressive lesions but spared in diabetic palsy?

faq.a: Ischemic palsies often improve over weeks; compressive causes usually need surgical decompression or aneurysm repair.
faq.q: Can a third‑nerve palsy resolve without surgery?

faq.a: A fixed, dilated pupil on the side of the herniation with a ‘down‑and‑out’ eye.
faq.q: What bedside sign suggests uncal herniation?

exam: A patient presents with painless ptosis and normal pupil size—what is the most likely mechanism? — Ischemic infarct of the oculomotor nucleus sparing peripheral parasympathetic fibers.
You see a painful, dilated pupil with limited eye movements—what urgent investigation is indicated? — Non‑contrast CT head to look for mass effect or aneurysm.
How does uncal herniation produce a fixed dilated pupil? — Temporal lobe pushes against the tentorial edge, compressing the peripheral parasympathetic fibers of CN III.
In a diabetic patient with third‑nerve palsy, why would you avoid immediate neurosurgical referral? — Pupil-sparing pattern suggests microvascular ischemia, which often resolves conservatively.

What maneuver helps differentiate a true third‑nerve palsy from a myasthenic crisis? — Ask the patient to look upward repeatedly; fatigue‑related weakness worsens in myasthenia, whereas a nerve lesion remains constant.

Why is CT angiography preferred over lumbar puncture in a suspected posterior communicating artery aneurysm? — Angiography visualises the aneurysm directly; LP risks worsening herniation and provides no vascular detail.
A child from a malaria‑endemic area has bilateral third‑nerve palsy—what tropical cause should you consider? — Cerebral malaria with basal meningitis affecting the cranial nerves.
What is the first step in managing a patient with suspected uncal herniation? — Raise the head of the bed, hyperventilate briefly, and arrange emergent neuro‑imaging.
ai.title: Oculomotor Nerve (Cranial Nerve III)
ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: The oculomotor nerve supplies most extra‑ocular muscles, levator palpebrae, and parasympathetic fibers to the pupil. Understanding its pathway, blood supply and common lesions helps clinicians diagnose life‑threatening brain herniation and aneurysm in low‑resource settings.

b: Motor: levator palpebrae, superior, medial, inferior rectus, inferior oblique
sections.p: Cranial nerve III emerges from the midbrain, passes between the posterior cerebral and superior cerebellar arteries, and enters the orbit via the superior orbital fissure.

b: Origin: Edinger‑Westphal (parasympathetic) and oculomotor nuclei (motor) in the dorsal midbrain
Course: Interpeduncular fossa → cavernous sinus → superior orbital fissure
sections.p: The nerve has a superficial peripheral motor core and a central parasympathetic core. It travels in the subarachnoid space, then the cavernous sinus, before reaching the orbit.

b: Close to posterior communicating artery—aneurysm risk
Vulnerable to uncal herniation compressing the nerve against the tentorial edge
sections.p: In the cavernous sinus the oculomotor nerve lies lateral to the internal carotid artery and is separated from CN IV, V1, V2, and VI.

b: Ischemic infarct of the midbrain nucleus → isolated motor palsy
Vasculitis (e.g., HIV‑related) can affect the cavernous segment
sections.p: Branches from the posterior cerebral artery and the superior cerebellar artery supply the nerve in the midbrain; the cavernous segment receives meningeal branches from the internal carotid.

b: Parasympathetic fibers are peripheral, making them first affected by compression
sections.p: Motor fibers arise from the oculomotor nucleus; parasympathetic fibers arise from the Edinger‑Westphal nucleus and travel with the nerve to the ciliary ganglion.

b: Lesion → ptosis, ‘down‑and‑out’ eye, diplopia, mydriasis, loss of near focus
sections.p: Controls eye elevation, adduction, depression, and intorsion; raises the upper eyelid; constricts pupil and enables accommodation.

b: Compressive palsy: pupil dilated, painful, often unilateral
Ischemic palsy: pupil spared, painless, often in diabetics
Uncal herniation: fixed dilated pupil, rapid deterioration
sections.p: Third‑nerve palsy can be compressive (aneurysm, uncal herniation) or ischemic (diabetes, hypertension). In low‑resource settings, aneurysm may present with painful ptosis and a dilated pupil; TB meningitis can cause basal meningitis affecting the nerve.

t.b: Detects mass effect, uncal herniation, or aneurysm; if unavailable, perform bedside pupil exam and assess for papilledema
Identifies posterior communicating artery aneurysm; if not available, refer for neurosurgical evaluation based on clinical suspicion

b: Ask patient to follow a moving finger in all directions; note limitation and diplopia
Check for ptosis by comparing eyelid height
Assess pupil size and light reaction in bright and dim light
sections.p: A focused cranial nerve exam can differentiate compressive from ischemic third‑nerve palsy and guide urgent management.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden unilateral dilated pupil with loss of eye movements
Rapidly decreasing level of consciousness with fixed dilated pupil
Severe retro‑orbital headache with third‑nerve palsy
